    i: dim in [0, NI)      # rows of A and C
    j: dim in [0, NJ)      # columns of B and C
    k: dim in [0, NK)      # columns of A / rows of B (reduction dimension)

data:

    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * NK + k

    # B: NK x NJ, stored *column-major* to favor k-innermost loops.
    # For fixed column j, elements B[k, j] are contiguous in k.
    B[k, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> j * NK + k  # column-major

    # C: NI x NJ, row-major
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NJ + j

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

    # Tunable blocking and SIMD parameters (chosen for the target machine)
    TI: int  # tile size along i (rows of C / A)
    TJ: int  # tile size along j (cols of C / B)
    TK: int  # tile size along k (reduction dim)
    VK: int  # SIMD width used when vectorizing the k-loop

computation:
    # GEMM kernel:
    #   C := beta * C + alpha * A * B
    #
    # Expressed in a single assignment so that for each (i, j) the
    # accumulator remains in a register across the k-reduction:
    #
    #   C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]
    #              + alpha * sum_{k=0..NK-1} A[i, k] * B[k, j]
    #
    # This is algebraically equivalent to the original two-phase code:
    #   C[i, j] *= beta;
    #   C[i, j] += alpha * sum_k A[i, k] * B[k, j];
    # but it avoids an extra pass over C and avoids repeated loads/stores
    # of C inside the k-loop.
    #
    # The reduction sum(k, ...) implies:
    #   - a loop over k for each fixed (i, j),
    #   - an implicit dependence along k for each (i, j),
    #   - full independence across different (i, j) pairs.
    gemm:
        for i, j:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] +
                       alpha * sum(k, A[i, k] * B[k, j])

optimization:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Three-dimensional blocking (tiling) for cache locality
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Tile the iteration space so that:
    #   - a TI x TJ tile of C and the corresponding rows/columns of A and B
    #     fit in L1/L2 cache,
    #   - TK controls the k-depth of each tile, trading off between temporal
    #     reuse and register pressure.
    #
    # Resulting tile shapes:
    #   - A tile: TI x TK
    #   - B tile: TK x TJ
    #   - C tile: TI x TJ
    block(i, I, TI)   # i = I * TI + i_inner
    block(j, J, TJ)   # j = J * TJ + j_inner
    block(k, K, TK)   # k = K * TK + k_inner

    # Hoist tile indices to form the loop nest:
    #   for I           // outer tiles over rows of C/A
    #     for J         // outer tiles over cols of C/B
    #       for K       // tiles along reduction dimension
    #         for i, j, k within the tile
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Parallelization
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Each (I, J) tile updates a distinct TI x TJ submatrix of C; tiles are
    # independent because:
    #   - A and B are read-only,
    #   - C tiles are disjoint in memory.
    #
    # Parallelize across I (and optionally J) to use many cores.
    parallelize(I)
    # Optionally, also parallelize across J (e.g., using loop collapsing)
    # when NI is not large enough to saturate all cores by itself.
    # parallelize(J)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. SIMD vectorization along the reduction dimension k
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Thanks to the chosen layouts:
    #   - A[i, k] is contiguous in k for each fixed i (row-major),
    #   - B[k, j] is contiguous in k for each fixed j (column-major),
    # making the k-loop ideal for SIMD vectorization.
    #
    # For each (i, j), the scalar dot product:
    #   sum_k A[i, k] * B[k, j]
    # is implemented as a vectorized loop over k in chunks of VK, accumulating
    # partial sums in vector registers, followed by a horizontal reduction.
    vectorize(k, VK)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Loop unrolling in the j-dimension within each tile
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Unroll j inside a tile to compute several C[i, j] values in parallel
    # and to better reuse A[i, k] across multiple columns of C:
    #
    #   for i in tile:
    #     for j in tile (unrolled by UJ):
    #       acc_j[0..UJ-1] = beta * C[i, j+offset]  // in registers
    #       for k in tile:
    #         a_ik = A[i, k]
    #         // see strength-reduction below for 'a_ik_scaled'
    #         acc_j[t] += alpha * a_ik * B[k, j+offset+t]
    #       C[i, j+offset+t] = acc_j[t]
    #
    # This encourages the compiler to keep multiple accumulators in registers
    # and to schedule FMAs efficiently.
    unroll(j, 4)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Arithmetic strength reduction and reuse
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Inside the innermost k-loop, the naive computation is:
    #   acc_ij += alpha * A[i, k] * B[k, j]
    #
    # For each fixed (i, k) within a tile, we can hoist the multiplication
    # by alpha out of the j-loop:
    #
    #   a_ik_scaled = alpha * A[i, k]    # once per (i, k)
    #   acc_ij      += a_ik_scaled * B[k, j]
    #
    # This:
    #   - eliminates one multiply per (i, k, j),
    #   - exposes a simple multiply-add pattern that maps directly to a
    #     fused multiply-add (FMA) instruction:
    #       acc_ij = fma(a_ik_scaled, B[k, j], acc_ij)
    #
    # Implement a_ik_scaled as a scalar temporary in a register (no extra
    # array allocation, thus no extra asymptotic memory footprint).

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Fused beta scaling of C with the GEMM update
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The high-level assignment:
    #
    #   C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] + alpha * sum(k, A[i, k] * B[k, j])
    #
    # replaces the original two passes:
    #   C[i, j] *= beta;
    #   C[i, j] += alpha * sum_k(...);
    #
    # Benefits:
    #   - C[i, j] is loaded once and stored once,
    #   - there is no separate "scaling-only" loop over C,
    #   - better opportunity to keep C[i, j] in a register during the entire
    #     k-reduction.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 7. Optional micro-kernel blocking within tiles
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # For further tuning on a specific x64 core, introduce a second level of
    # very small blocking inside each (i, j) tile, e.g.:
    #
    #   block(i, Ii, 4)
    #   block(j, Jj, 8)
    #   unroll(i, 4)
    #   unroll(j, 8)
    #
    # so that each 4x8 micro-tile of C is computed entirely in registers
    # before being written back to memory. This exploits the wide SIMD units
    # and the large register file typical of modern x64 cores, while the
    # outer (I, J, K) tiles manage cache locality.

domain:
    # Logical iteration space of the GEMM kernel.
    i: dim in [0, NI)   # row index of A and C
    j: dim in [0, NJ)   # column index of B and C
    k: dim in [0, NK)   # reduction index (shared dimension of A and B)

data:
    # All matrices are stored in row-major layout, consistent with the C code.
    # The affine expressions give the element's linear offset from the base.
    A[i, k]: in    DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * NK + k     # A is NI x NK
    B[k, j]: in    DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * NJ + j     # B is NK x NJ
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NJ + j     # C is NI x NJ

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

    # Tunable blocking parameters for cache hierarchy (chosen at compile-time
    # or runtime; values below are recommendations for a modern x64 machine).
    TI: int  # tile size along i (rows of A, C)      e.g., TI = 64..128
    TJ: int  # tile size along j (cols of B, C)      e.g., TJ = 64..128
    TK: int  # tile size along k (reduction dim)     e.g., TK = 64..256

    # SIMD and unrolling parameters (micro-kernel configuration).
    VEC_J: int  # SIMD vector width along j (e.g., 8 for AVX2 doubles)
    UI:    int  # unroll factor along i inside a tile (e.g., 4)
    UK:    int  # unroll factor along k inside a tile (e.g., 4)

computation:
    gemm:
        # Semantics: for every (i, j),
        #   C[i,j] = beta * C[i,j] + alpha * sum_{k=0..NK-1} A[i,k] * B[k,j]
        #
        # This single assignment is mathematically equivalent to the original
        # PolyBench kernel, which first scales C by beta and then accumulates
        # alpha * A * B into C.
        for i, j:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] + alpha * sum(k, A[i, k] * B[k, j])

optimization:
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. High-level loop structure and locality
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # We implement the above computation with a blocked 3D loop nest to exploit
    # temporal locality in A, B, and C and to match the cache hierarchy.
    #
    # Target logical loop order after transformations:
    #
    #   for I in 0 .. ceil(NI / TI):              # tile index in i
    #     for J in 0 .. ceil(NJ / TJ):            # tile index in j
    #       parallel over (I,J)
    #       # Work on a TI x TJ tile of C at a time
    #       for K in 0 .. ceil(NK / TK):          # tile index in k
    #         for i in tile I:
    #           for k in tile K:
    #             aik = alpha * A[i,k]            # scalar replacement
    #             for j in tile J (vectorized):
    #               # fused multiply-add into C
    #               C[i,j] = beta * C[i,j]  (only once per (i,j))  +
    #                          sum over all K-tiles of (aik * B[k,j])
    #
    # The directives below describe this schedule.

    # 3D blocking (tiling) for cache reuse: split each dimension into
    # an outer tile index (I,J,K) and an inner index (i,j,k).
    block(i, I, TI)   # I indexes tiles of TI consecutive rows of A and C
    block(j, J, TJ)   # J indexes tiles of TJ consecutive columns of B and C
    block(k, K, TK)   # K indexes tiles of TK elements along the reduction dim

    # Hoist tile loops to the outermost level so we iterate over tiles of C
    # and K-tiles of A,B before iterating over individual elements.
    # Resulting loop order (outermost -> innermost) is:
    #   I, J, K, i, k, j
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # Within each (I, J) C-tile, each (i, j) element of C is updated
    # independently over all k, so the computation over different tiles of C
    # can run in parallel without synchronization.
    #
    # We parallelize across tiles in I (rows). On a machine with many cores and
    # very large NJ, extending to 2D tile parallelism (I and J) is possible.
    parallelize(I)
    #parallelize(J)  # optional: 2D tile parallelism if NI is small and NJ large

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. SIMD vectorization and micro-kernel
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Make the innermost loop run along j, which is contiguous in memory for
    # both C[i,*] and B[k,*] (row-major), enabling efficient SIMD.
    #
    # The prior hoisting and blocking give innermost loops over (i,k,j);
    # we keep j as the innermost dimension inside the tile.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)

    # Unroll short inner loops to form a small register-blocked micro-kernel
    # (e.g., computing UI x VEC_J elements of C in registers).
    unroll(i, UI)
    unroll(k, UK)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Arithmetic strength reduction and scalar replacement
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The expression alpha * A[i,k] does not depend on j and is reused across
    # the inner j loop of the blocked nest. We ensure it is computed only once
    # per (i,k) and kept in a scalar register.
    #
    # New directive (explained by this comment):
    #   scalar_replace(expr, scope, reused_across)
    #     - expr: expression to cache
    #     - scope: indices over which expr is defined once
    #     - reused_across: indices over which the cached value is reused
    scalar_replace(expr = alpha * A[i, k],
                   scope = (i, k),
                   reused_across = j)

    # Use fused multiply-add when available:
    #   C[i,j] = C[i,j] + aik * B[k,j]
    # becomes a single FMA instruction, reducing latency and improving
    # numerical accuracy (fewer rounding steps).
    #
    # New directive (explained by this comment):
    #   use_fma(update): implement the given update as a fused multiply-add.
    use_fma(update = C[i, j] += (alpha * A[i, k]) * B[k, j])

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Data alignment (implementation detail, not semantic)
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Ensure matrices are allocated with 64-byte alignment to match cache-line
    # and SIMD alignment on modern x64, improving load/store efficiency.
    #
    # New directive:
    #   align(array, bytes): request that 'array' be aligned to 'bytes'.
    align(A, 64)
    align(B, 64)
    align(C, 64)

    TK: int  # block size along k (shared inner dimension)

    # Tuning knobs for SIMD and ILP (instruction-level parallelism).
    VJ: int  # SIMD width along j (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double, 16 for AVX-512 float)
    UI: int  # unroll factor along i inside a tile

computation:
    # GEMM semantics:
    #   C := beta * C + alpha * A * B
    #
    # Expressed element-wise, matching the math of the original kernel:
    #   C[i,j] = beta * C[i,j] + alpha * sum_k A[i,k] * B[k,j]
    #
    # (The original C code computes this via an outer scale by beta,
    #  followed by the triple-nested accumulation; this fused form is
    #  mathematically equivalent.)
    for i, j:
        C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] + alpha * sum(k, A[i, k] * B[k, j])

optimization:
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Three-dimensional blocking (tiling) for cache locality
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Split each logical loop dimension into an outer tile index (uppercase)
    # and an inner in-tile index (lowercase), with tile sizes TI, TJ, TK.
    #
    # i = I * TI + i_in   where i_in ≡ i (the renamed inner dim)
    # j = J * TJ + j_in
    # k = K * TK + k_in
    #
    # Remainder tiles (on the edges) are handled by partial tiles of smaller size.
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)
    block(k, K, TK)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Loop reordering (schedule) to operate on a C tile at a time
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Target schedule (conceptually):
    #
    # for I:                      # outer tiles in i (rows)
    #   for J:                    # outer tiles in j (cols)
    #     # Load & beta-scale a TI×TJ tile of C into C_tile
    #     for i (inside tile I):
    #       for j (inside tile J):
    #         C_tile[i, j] = beta * C[I*TI + i, J*TJ + j]
    #
    #     # Accumulate contributions from the entire K dimension in blocks
    #     for K:
    #       for k (inside tile K):
    #         for i (inside tile I):
    #           a_ik = alpha * A[I*TI + i, K*TK + k]    # hoisted per-(i,k)
    #           for j (inside tile J):
    #             C_tile[i, j] += a_ik * B[K*TK + k, J*TJ + j]
    #
    #     # Write completed tile back to global C
    #     for i (inside tile I):
    #       for j (inside tile J):
    #         C[I*TI + i, J*TJ + j] = C_tile[i, j]
    #
    # This schedule:
    #   - Keeps a TI×TJ block of C in registers/L1 while sweeping over k.
    #   - Reads and writes each C element exactly once.
    #   - Reuses A and B blocks from faster caches.
    #
    # We express this intent by hoisting the tile indices outward:
    hoist(I)  # make I the outermost loop
    hoist(J)  # nest J immediately inside I
    hoist(K)  # nest K just inside (I, J), outside the inner i/j/k loops

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Parallelization
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # All (i, j) pairs are independent; consequently, each (I, J) tile of C
    # is independent. We parallelize across the outer tile loops.
    #
    # The runtime may map (I, J) tiles to threads in a 1D or 2D partitioning,
    # e.g., collapse(I, J) and distribute, but semantically:
    #   - No synchronization is needed between different (I, J) tiles.
    #   - Each thread works on disjoint rows/columns of C.
    parallelize(I)   # primary parallel dimension: tiles over rows of C

    # Optionally also expose J for 2D tiling across threads, if desired.
    # (This is safe as long as the parallel runtime does not create nested
    #  parallel regions that oversubscribe cores.)
    parallelize(J)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. SIMD vectorization along j (inner-most column index)
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # In row-major layout:
    #   - For both B and C, the j index is contiguous in memory.
    #   - Vectorizing along j (the in-tile 'j' after blocking) gives
    #     unit-stride accesses for C and B and good use of SIMD units.
    #
    # The vectorization width VJ is tuned to the ISA (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double).
    vectorize(j, VJ)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Loop unrolling for ILP and FMA utilization
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Unroll the inner i loop (rows within a tile) to expose ILP and allow
    # the compiler to map multiple independent accumulators to registers.
    unroll(i, UI)
    # Additionally unroll the inner k loop in the micro-kernel; a small fixed
    # factor (e.g., 4 or 8) works well in practice and is easily tuned.
    unroll(k, 4)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Use of local accumulation variables and strength reduction
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Inside the innermost micro-kernel (after tiling and scheduling), the
    # compiler is instructed/allowed to:
    #
    # - Use a local accumulator per (i, j) entry in the current tile:
    #       acc_ij = beta * C[i, j]
    #       acc_ij += alpha * sum_k A[i, k] * B[k, j]
    #       C[i, j] = acc_ij
    #   or equivalently with the C_tile buffer:
    #       C_tile[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]
    #       C_tile[i, j] += alpha * sum_k A[i, k] * B[k, j]
    #       C[i, j] = C_tile[i, j]
    #
    #   This ensures:
    #     * Each C[i, j] is loaded once, stored once.
    #     * All k-contributions are accumulated in registers.
    #
    # - Hoist alpha * A[i, k] out of the innermost j loop:
    #       a_ik = alpha * A[i, k]
    #       for j:
    #           C_tile[i, j] += a_ik * B[k, j]
    #
    #   This replaces multiple multiplications by alpha with a single one
    #   per (i, k) pair and reuses a_ik for all j, which is exactly the
    #   optimization a good compiler will derive from this schedule.
    #
    # These transformations are consistent with the high-level assignment
    #   C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] + alpha * sum(k, A[i, k] * B[k, j])
    # and do not change the mathematical result (only the order of FP
    # operations and thus round-off at machine precision).

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 7. Memory usage constraints and layout
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # - The only additional storage is the per-tile C_tile[ii, jj], whose
    #   size is TI × TJ and thus negligible compared to A, B, and C.
    #   This increases total memory usage by << 50%.
    #
    # - The global layouts of A, B, and C remain row-major and unchanged
    #   relative to the original C code, so no changes to initialization
    #   or I/O are required.
